w: Legend credits Dido, a Tyrian princess fleeing east, with founding Carthage here in 814 BC - New City, Qart Hadasht, born to trade rather than conquest. These ports were the engine room of a thalassocracy that ran the western Mediterranean for centuries, until Rome ended it for good.
s: The old harbour of an empire built on trade
_facts: Carthage founded, per legend, by Dido, a Tyrian princess, around 814 BC
Carthage was a thalassocracy - an empire based on sea trade
The ports controlled the western Mediterranean until conflict with the Roman Republic ended it

w: Perched on Byrsa Hill, this former cathedral was raised directly over the ruins of a temple to Eshmun, the Punic god of healing - the old foundations can still be reached from the basement. Deconsecrated and renamed the Acropolium in 1993, it now hosts concerts instead of Mass.
s: A cathedral built over a Punic god's temple
_facts: Built atop the ruins of a temple to Eshmun, the Punic god of healing
The old foundations can still be reached from the basement
Renamed the Acropolium in 1993, no longer used for worship, now hosts concerts and public events

n: Cathedral of St. Vincent de Paul
w: Cardinal Lavigerie laid a first stone for a pro-cathedral here in 1881; poor ground conditions killed it, so this one rose instead - a mashup of Moorish revival, Gothic revival and Neo-Byzantine styles, opened Christmas Day 1897. Money ran out before the belltowers; concrete towers went up in 1910.
s: Moorish revival meets Gothic meets Byzantium
_facts: Mixture of Moorish revival, Gothic revival and Neo-Byzantine styles
Opened Christmas 1897 without belltowers due to shortage of funds
Reinforced concrete towers completed 1910 using the Hennebique technique
Cardinal Charles Lavigerie laid the first stone for an earlier pro-cathedral in 1881

w: A Spanish governor rebuilt this lagoon island's Roman citadel into Fort Santiago Chikly between 1546 and 1550; it was abandoned by 1830 and left to crumble. Digs in the 1990s turned up Roman and Byzantine mosaics beneath the ramparts. Today the ruin doubles as a nesting ground for little egrets.
s: A Spanish fort on a Roman ruin, now an egret colony
_facts: Fort Santiago Chikly, a former Roman citadel, rebuilt by the Spanish 1546-1550
Abandoned in 1830, declared national cultural heritage 1993
1990s excavations found Roman and Byzantine mosaics
Now a nesting ground for little egrets

w: Gate of the Sea, or Porte de France - the threshold where the walled medina gives way to the boulevards of colonial Ville Nouvelle. Its crenellated archway has been rebuilt and altered so many times over the centuries that it now reads more as a hinge between two cities than a relic of one.
s: The gate where the old city meets the new
_facts: Marks the separation between the medina and the modern city
Also known as Porte De France
Current form is an archway topped by a crenellated parapet

w: The Carthaginians called it the Mountain of the Two Horns and considered it sacred ground - rituals here were dedicated to Baal Hammon, the horned god. Its twin Jurassic-limestone peaks, pine- and cedar-covered, now anchor a national park overlooking the Gulf of Tunis, the same view its ancient worshippers once had.
s: The sacred 'two-horned mountain' of ancient Carthage
_facts: Name means 'Mountain of the Two-Horned', originally from the Punic language
Considered sacred in ancient Carthage, site of rituals for the god Baal Hammon
Part of Boukornine National Park, covered in Aleppo pine and cedar

w: Combining a working mosque with a türbe - a mausoleum wing - in one Ottoman-era complex, this is an official historical monument in the heart of Tunis: one more of the medina's stack of centuries-old religious foundations still standing exactly where they were built.
s: A mosque and mausoleum in one, since Ottoman times
_facts: Combines a mosque with a türbe (mausoleum)
Official historical monument

w: It opened on 20 November 1902 under a different name entirely - the Municipal Casino of Tunis - before settling into life as the capital's grand Art Nouveau stage for opera, ballet and symphony. More than a century on, it still sits on the city's central avenue, doing the job it was quietly renamed for.
s: Opened in 1902 as a casino, not a stage
_facts: Built in Art Nouveau style, opened 20 November 1902
Originally called the Municipal Casino of Tunis
Showcases opera, ballet, symphonic concerts and drama

w: Tunis's Grand Synagogue sits on Avenue de la Liberte under a second, stranger name - the Temple of Osiris - a relic of a Jewish community that once anchored this stretch of the city. Its congregation is smaller now, but the building still holds the name and the history.
s: Also known, oddly, as the Temple of Osiris
_facts: Also called the Temple of Osiris
Located on Avenue de la Liberte

w: Before Youssef Dey consecrated it as a mosque in 1631 - the first Ottoman one built in Tunis, and the eleventh in the capital overall - this space served as a public speaking venue. Ali Bey ordered a thorough restoration in the late 1800s; a 1926 decree folded it into the University of Ez-Zitouna.
s: Tunis's first Ottoman mosque, once a public podium
_facts: First Ottoman mosque built in Tunis, 11th mosque built in the capital
Operated as a public speaking venue before becoming a mosque under Youssef Dey in 1631
Restored in the late 19th century under Ali Bey
1926 decree made it an annex of the University of Ez-Zitouna

w: Thirty-seven square kilometres of lagoon separate the capital from the open Gulf of Tunis - shallow enough, in places, to wade. It was once the city's natural harbour, the reason Tunis exists exactly where it does, before ships outgrew it and the modern port moved on.
s: The shallow lagoon that was once Tunis's harbour
_facts: 37 square kilometre natural lagoon between Tunis and the Gulf of Tunis
Very shallow in depth
Was once the natural harbour of Tunis

w: A UNESCO World Heritage quarter since 1979, the old walled medina packs in some 700 monuments - palaces, mosques, mausoleums, madrasas, fountains - laid down across centuries and still functioning as a living neighbourhood rather than a museum piece.
s: 700 monuments packed into one walled quarter
_facts: UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979
Contains around 700 monuments including palaces, mosques, mausoleums, madrasas and fountains

w: Long before Rome finished it off, a walled citadel called Byrsa crowned this hill above Carthage's Phoenician harbour - gone now, but the hill still carries its name, and still looks out over the site of the empire it once guarded.
s: The citadel hill above Carthage's vanished harbour
_facts: Byrsa was a walled citadel above the Phoenician harbour in ancient Carthage
Gave its name to the hill it stood on

w: Founded in 1885 as the French Library, then renamed the People's Library, Tunisia's legal-deposit archive finally got a home worthy of it in 2005 - a 46-metre, 14-floor tower built in a proudly Islamic-revival style, one of the tallest buildings in the country.
s: A 14-floor library in full Islamic-revival dress
_facts: Founded 1885 as the French Library, later the People's Library
Relocated to a new 46m, 14-floor building in 2005
One of the tallest buildings in Tunisia, in Islamic-style architecture

w: Abu Zakariya Yahya, the first ruler of the Hafsid dynasty, commissioned this mosque between 1230 and 1233 to serve as the main Friday mosque of the Kasbah district - a foundation stone of the dynasty that would go on to rule Tunis for the next three centuries.
s: Founded in the 1230s by Tunisia's first Hafsid ruler
_facts: Built 1230-1233 on the orders of Abu Zakariya Yahya, the first Hafsid ruler
Serves as the main Friday mosque of the Kasbah district
